filters.name: Align by Bounding Box
filters.shortDescription: Coarsely align one layer to another by matching their oriented bounding boxes.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Aligns the source layer to the reference by fitting their **oriented bounding boxes**. It needs no initial guess and no correspondences, and it is fast, which makes it the natural first step before ICP — *Align by ICP* can run it for you.

An oriented bounding box is only defined up to 180-degree flips about its axes, so the fit is ambiguous in principle. TrueForm resolves this by testing the candidate orientations against a spatial index of the reference and keeping the best.

The result is written to the source layer's **matrix**; vertex coordinates are not touched.

Implemented with TrueForm's `fit_obb_alignment`.

parameters.label: Source Layer
parameters.help: The layer that is moved.

parameters.label: Reference Layer
parameters.help: The layer that stays put.

filters.name: Align by ICP (TrueForm)
filters.shortDescription: Align one layer to another with iterative closest point, point-to-point or point-to-plane.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Refines the alignment of the source layer onto the reference by **iterative closest point**.

**Metric** chooses the error being minimised:

- *Point to point* — the classic formulation. Robust, but converges slowly across flat regions where many correspondences are nearly equivalent.
- *Point to plane* — measures each correspondence along the reference's surface normal, so the source can slide freely along a surface. It converges in far fewer iterations on smooth geometry, and is the better default when the reference has reliable normals.

ICP only refines **locally**: from a poor starting position it converges confidently to the wrong answer rather than failing. **Coarse Initialization** therefore runs *Align by Bounding Box* first, which is usually enough to land in the right basin.

**Samples** subsamples the source each iteration, which is what keeps large clouds tractable; 0 uses every point. **Outlier Proportion** discards that fraction of the worst correspondences each iteration, which matters when the two layers only partly overlap.

The reported **Chamfer residual** is the mean one-way distance after alignment — useful for comparing runs.

The result is written to the source layer's **matrix**; vertex coordinates are not touched.

Implemented with TrueForm's `fit_icp_alignment`.

parameters.label: Source Layer
parameters.help: The layer that is moved.

parameters.label: Reference Layer
parameters.help: The layer that stays put.

parameters.label: Metric
parameters.help: Point to plane converges faster on smooth surfaces; point to point is safer when the reference normals are unreliable.

parameters.label: Coarse Initialization
parameters.help: Run a bounding-box alignment first. Leave on unless the layers are already roughly registered.

parameters.label: Max Iterations
parameters.help: Upper bound on ICP iterations.

parameters.label: Samples
parameters.help: Source points sampled per iteration. 0 uses all of them, which is slower but deterministic.

parameters.label: Min Relative Improvement
parameters.help: Stop once the error improves by less than this fraction between iterations.

parameters.label: Outlier Proportion
parameters.help: Fraction of the worst correspondences rejected each iteration. Raise it when the two layers only partly overlap.

filters.name: Align to Corresponding Points
filters.shortDescription: Align two layers whose vertices already correspond one to one, optionally solving for scale.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Computes the transformation that best maps the source layer's vertices onto the reference's, assuming the two are already in **one-to-one correspondence**: same number of live vertices, in matching order. This is the Procrustes (Kabsch) fit.

Use it when the correspondence is known by construction — two states of the same mesh, a mesh and its deformed copy, or point sets you have paired yourself. When the correspondence is unknown, use *Align by ICP* instead, which searches for it.

**Allow Uniform Scale** is the reason to reach for this filter over ICP: with correspondences given, scale can be solved for as well as rotation and translation, which no ICP variant here does. Leave it off for a rigid fit.

The result is written to the source layer's **matrix**; vertex coordinates are not touched.

Implemented with TrueForm's `fit_rigid_alignment` and `fit_similarity_alignment`.

parameters.label: Source Layer
parameters.help: The layer that is moved.

parameters.label: Reference Layer
parameters.help: The layer that stays put.

parameters.label: Allow Uniform Scale
parameters.help: Also solve for a single scale factor. Only possible because the correspondences are given rather than searched for.

filters.name: Mesh Union (TrueForm)
filters.shortDescription: Exact boolean union of two layers.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
The union of two closed solids: everything inside either one.

TrueForm evaluates booleans with **exact predicates**, so coplanar faces and near-degenerate intersections are decided consistently rather than by a tolerance. Both layers are taken in **world space**, so their layer matrices are applied first, and the result is added as a new layer with an identity matrix.

The libigl implementation of the same operation is also available and worth comparing on difficult input.

parameters.label: First Layer
parameters.help: The first operand.

parameters.label: Second Layer
parameters.help: The second operand.

TrueForm evaluates booleans with **exact predicates**, so coplanar faces and near-degenerate intersections are decided consistently rather than by a tolerance. Both layers are taken in **world space**, so their layer matrices are applied first, and the result is added as a new layer with an identity matrix.

The libigl implementation of the same operation is also available and worth comparing on difficult input.

filters.name: Mesh Difference (TrueForm)
filters.shortDescription: Exact boolean difference of two layers.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
The first solid with the second removed from it. Order matters: swap the two layers to get the opposite difference.

TrueForm evaluates booleans with **exact predicates**, so coplanar faces and near-degenerate intersections are decided consistently rather than by a tolerance. Both layers are taken in **world space**, so their layer matrices are applied first, and the result is added as a new layer with an identity matrix.

The libigl implementation of the same operation is also available and worth comparing on difficult input.

parameters.label: Layer to Cut
parameters.help: The first operand.

parameters.label: Layer to Subtract
parameters.help: The second operand.

filters.name: Mesh Symmetric Difference (TrueForm)
filters.shortDescription: Exact boolean symmetric difference of two layers.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Everything inside exactly one of the two solids, and nothing inside both.

TrueForm's boolean primitive offers union, intersection and difference but not this one, so it is evaluated through the CSG evaluator as `(A - B) | (B - A)`. The result is the same; only the route differs.

TrueForm evaluates booleans with **exact predicates**, so coplanar faces and near-degenerate intersections are decided consistently rather than by a tolerance. Both layers are taken in **world space**, so their layer matrices are applied first, and the result is added as a new layer with an identity matrix.

The libigl implementation of the same operation is also available and worth comparing on difficult input.

parameters.label: First Layer
parameters.help: The first operand.

parameters.label: Second Layer
parameters.help: The second operand.

filters.name: Mesh CSG Expression
filters.shortDescription: Evaluate a boolean expression over any number of layers in one exact pass.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Evaluates an arbitrary constructive-solid-geometry expression over the document's layers, in a **single arrangement** rather than a chain of pairwise booleans. That matters for more than convenience: chaining booleans re-meshes and re-intersects at every step, accumulating error and cost, while one arrangement resolves all the surfaces together and classifies each region once.

**Operands are layer numbers**, as shown in the layer panel. Operators, loosest-binding first:

| Operator | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `\|` | union |
| `-` | difference |
| `&` | intersection |
| `~` | complement |

`|` and `-` share the lowest precedence and associate to the left; `&` binds tighter; `~` binds tightest. Parentheses group.

Examples:

- `0 | 1 | 2` — the union of three layers
- `(0 | 1) - 2` — two layers joined, then a third drilled out of them
- `0 & ~1` — the part of layer 0 outside layer 1, i.e. the difference

A layer may appear more than once; it becomes a single operand. Every referenced layer is taken in world space.

parameters.label: Expression
parameters.help: A boolean expression over layer numbers, e.g. (0 | 1) - 2. Operators: | union, - difference, & intersection, ~ complement.

filters.name: Extract Outer Shell
filters.shortDescription: Keep only the outermost surface of a layer, discarding internal shells.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Resolves the layer's self-intersections and keeps only the **outermost** boundary, dropping every internal shell and any surface enclosed by another.

This is the repair step for geometry assembled from overlapping parts — kitbashed models, scans merged from several pieces, or anything destined for 3D printing, where interior walls are invisible but still slow slicing and can confuse a slicer about what is solid.

The input should be solid rather than an open sheet: an open surface has no inside, so there is no outer shell to extract.

parameters.label: Layer
parameters.help: The layer to extract the outer shell from.

filters.name: Create Polyline from Self-Intersections
filters.shortDescription: Extract the curve where a mesh passes through itself, as a polyline layer.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Extracts the exact curve along which the layer intersects **itself**, as a new polyline layer.

*Select Self Intersecting Faces* marks the faces involved; this gives the intersection itself, which is what you need to see where the problem is rather than merely that it exists — and, being exact geometry rather than a selection, it can be measured, exported, or swept into a tube.

A clean mesh produces nothing, and the filter says so.

parameters.label: Layer
parameters.help: The layer to examine.

filters.name: Create Polyline from Mesh Intersection
filters.shortDescription: Extract the curve where two layers cross, as a polyline layer.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Extracts the exact curve along which two layers intersect, as a new polyline layer. Both are taken in world space, so their layer matrices are applied first.

The curve is computed with the same exact arrangement the booleans use, so it is the true intersection rather than a sampled approximation, and it is usable as a construction line — a seam to cut along, a profile to sweep, or a measurement.

Layers that do not touch produce nothing.

parameters.label: First Layer
parameters.help: The first layer.

parameters.label: Second Layer
parameters.help: The second layer.

filters.name: Create Polyline from Scalar Isocontour
filters.shortDescription: Extract contour lines of the per-vertex scalar field as polylines on the surface.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Extracts level sets of the **per-vertex scalar field** as polylines lying exactly on the surface.

This turns every scalar QMeshLab can compute into something with extractable contours: geodesic distance from a point or a border, curvature, ambient occlusion, shape diameter, raster coverage, or anything written by *Compute Vertex Scalar by Expression*. Contours of a geodesic distance are isodistance rings; of a height field, topographic contour lines.

**Contours** sets how many levels are extracted. They are spaced evenly and placed strictly *inside* the range, never at its extremes, where a contour is either empty or the whole boundary.

By default the range is the field's own minimum and maximum. Enable **Use Custom Range** to contour a chosen band instead — useful when a few outliers would otherwise compress every contour into a corner of the model.

A constant field has no contours, and the filter says so rather than returning an empty layer.

parameters.label: Layer
parameters.help: The layer whose scalar field is contoured.

parameters.label: Contours
parameters.help: How many evenly spaced contour levels to extract.

parameters.label: Use Custom Range
parameters.help: Contour a chosen value band instead of the field's full min-max range.

parameters.label: Min
parameters.help: Lower end of the contoured range. Ignored unless Use Custom Range is on.

parameters.label: Max
parameters.help: Upper end of the contoured range. Ignored unless Use Custom Range is on.

filters.name: Create Tube from Polyline
filters.shortDescription: Sweep a circular profile along a polyline to make a solid tube.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Sweeps a circular profile along each path of a polyline layer, producing a solid tube.

The *Create Polyline* filters produce edge meshes, which render as hairlines and cannot be shaded, exported to a solid format, or printed. This turns one into geometry — so a measured cross-section, an intersection seam, or a set of isocontours becomes something you can look at properly or fabricate.

**Radius** is the tube radius and **Sides** the number of segments around it; 8 is smooth enough for most uses, more for close-ups.

Edges are chained into paths first. A vertex where three or more edges meet cannot be swept unambiguously, so the polyline is **split** there rather than branched, and the count of such junctions is reported.

parameters.label: Polyline Layer
parameters.help: An edge-mesh layer, such as one made by the Create Polyline filters.

parameters.label: Radius
parameters.help: Radius of the swept profile.

parameters.label: Sides
parameters.help: Number of segments around the tube. Higher is smoother and heavier.

filters.name: Compute Signed Distance to Mesh
filters.shortDescription: Store each vertex's signed distance to another layer's surface in vertex scalar.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Writes, for every vertex, its distance to the nearest point of the reference layer's surface — **negative inside, positive outside**.

The sign is what makes this a field rather than a proximity readout. It can be contoured with *Create Polyline from Scalar Isocontour* (the zero contour is the intersection curve), thresholded to select a shell of given thickness, or used to measure how far a simplified or reconstructed model departs from its original and in which direction.

Both layers are taken in world space. The reference must be a **closed surface** for the sign to mean anything; on an open sheet the inside is undefined and the sign follows the surface orientation instead.

Enable **Unsigned** for absolute distance, which is what you want when only proximity matters.

Compare with *Hausdorff Distance*, which reports a single worst-case number, and *Measure Chamfer Distance*, which reports a mean.

parameters.label: Layer
parameters.help: The layer whose vertices are measured.

parameters.label: Reference Surface
parameters.help: The closed surface distances are measured to.

parameters.label: Unsigned
parameters.help: Store absolute distance, discarding inside/outside.

filters.name: Select Vertices Inside Mesh
filters.shortDescription: Select the vertices enclosed by another layer.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Selects every vertex that falls **inside** the enclosing layer's volume.

This is the spatial counterpart to selecting by an attribute: crop a scan to a region of interest by modelling a rough box or sphere around it, isolate the part of an assembly within a clearance envelope, or find geometry that has ended up inside a shell it should be outside of.

Containment is decided by the **sign of the distance** to the enclosing surface rather than by counting ray crossings, so a vertex lying exactly on the surface is resolved consistently instead of depending on the direction a ray happens to be cast.

The enclosing layer must be **closed** for inside to be meaningful. Enable **Select Outside** to invert the test.

parameters.label: Layer
parameters.help: The layer whose vertices are selected.

parameters.label: Enclosing Layer
parameters.help: The closed layer that defines inside.

parameters.label: Select Outside
parameters.help: Select the vertices outside the enclosing layer instead.

parameters.label: Mode
parameters.help: Replace the current selection, or add to and subtract from it.

filters.name: Measure Chamfer Distance
filters.shortDescription: Report the mean nearest-point distance between two layers.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Reports the **mean** distance from each vertex of one layer to the nearest vertex of the other.

Where the *Hausdorff Distance* reports the single worst correspondence — and so is dominated by one stray vertex — the chamfer distance averages over all of them. That makes it the more useful number for scoring an overall fit: comparing simplification settings, judging whether a registration improved, or tracking a reconstruction against ground truth. Use Hausdorff when the worst case is what matters, and this when the typical case is.

The measure is **not symmetric**: the mean distance from A to B differs from B to A, and a subset of a surface can sit very close to it while the surface as a whole sits far from the subset. **Symmetric** measures both directions and also reports the larger, which is the honest single number.

**Outlier Proportion** discards that fraction of the worst correspondences before averaging, for partial overlaps.

This measures vertex to vertex, so it is sensitive to how densely each layer is sampled.

parameters.label: Layer
parameters.help: The layer being measured.

parameters.label: Reference Layer
parameters.help: The layer measured against.

parameters.label: Symmetric
parameters.help: Measure both directions and report the larger.

parameters.label: Outlier Proportion
parameters.help: Fraction of the worst correspondences discarded before averaging.

filters.name: Smooth Vertices by Laplacian (TrueForm)
filters.shortDescription: Move each vertex towards the average of its neighbours.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Moves each vertex towards the average position of its linked neighbours, repeatedly.

**Lambda** is how far towards that average each step travels: 1.0 goes all the way, smaller values creep. **Iterations** is how many steps.

Laplacian smoothing **shrinks**: every step pulls the surface towards its own average, so a closed shape loses volume and sharp features round off. That is the price of its simplicity, and the reason for its Taubin sibling, which alternates a shrinking step with an expanding one to compensate.

Enable **Selected Only** to restrict movement to the current vertex selection.

Competing implementation: QMeshLab already has vcglib smoothing under *Geometry/Smoothing*. TrueForm's is parallelised through oneTBB, which shows on large meshes. Results should agree closely; where they differ the difference is in the boundary handling.

parameters.label: Iterations
parameters.help: How many smoothing steps to take.

parameters.label: Lambda
parameters.help: How far each step moves towards the neighbour average, 0 to 1.

parameters.label: Selected Only
parameters.help: Move only the selected vertices.

filters.name: Smooth Vertices by Taubin (TrueForm)
filters.shortDescription: Smooth without the shrinkage that Laplacian smoothing causes.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Alternates a Laplacian shrinking step with a slightly larger expanding one, so noise is removed while the overall volume is preserved. This is the smoothing to reach for by default; plain Laplacian is the one to reach for when you *want* the shape to contract.

**Lambda** is the shrinking step and **Kpb** sets the expanding one — larger Kpb pushes back harder against shrinkage. The defaults are the values from Taubin's paper and are a reasonable starting point.

Enable **Selected Only** to restrict movement to the current vertex selection.

Competing implementation: QMeshLab already has vcglib smoothing under *Geometry/Smoothing*. TrueForm's is parallelised through oneTBB, which shows on large meshes. Results should agree closely; where they differ the difference is in the boundary handling.

parameters.label: Iterations
parameters.help: How many smoothing steps to take.

parameters.label: Lambda
parameters.help: The shrinking step size, 0 to 1.

parameters.label: Kpb
parameters.help: Controls the compensating expansion. Larger values resist shrinkage more.

parameters.label: Selected Only
parameters.help: Move only the selected vertices.

filters.name: Compute Curvature (TrueForm)
filters.shortDescription: Estimate principal curvatures by local fitting and store one measure in vertex scalar.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Fits a local surface around each vertex over its k-ring neighbourhood and derives the two principal curvatures, then stores the chosen measure in **vertex scalar**.

**Measure** selects what is written:

| Measure | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Mean | (k1 + k2) / 2 |
| Gaussian | k1 * k2 — positive on domes and bowls, negative on saddles |
| Minimum / Maximum | the individual principal curvatures |
| Shape index | scale-free descriptor of local shape, from cup through saddle to cap |

**Ring** is the neighbourhood radius in rings of adjacent vertices. Larger values smooth the estimate and cost more; it is the knob to turn when noise dominates the result.

The shape index is worth knowing about: unlike the curvature values it is **independent of scale**, so it describes the *kind* of shape at a point rather than how strongly curved it is, which makes it comparable across models of different sizes.

Competing implementation: see also *Compute Curvature (Discrete)*, *(APSS)* and *(RIMLS)*.

parameters.label: Measure
parameters.help: Which curvature measure to store in vertex scalar.

parameters.label: Ring
parameters.help: Neighbourhood radius in vertex rings. Larger is smoother and slower.

filters.name: Compute Normals (TrueForm)
filters.shortDescription: Recompute per-vertex or per-face normals from the geometry.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Recomputes normals from the current geometry, either one per face or one per vertex (area-weighted from the incident faces).

Normals are computed in world space and mapped back through the layer matrix, so a layer carrying a non-uniform scale gets correct normals rather than merely rotated ones.

Competing implementation: *Compute Vertex Normals* and *Compute Face Normals* do the same with vcglib. This one is parallelised.

parameters.label: Target
parameters.help: Whether to write per-vertex or per-face normals.
